'''Jerome V. Moloney''' is an [[Irish Americans|Irish-American]] professor of [[optical sciences]] and [[mathematics]] at the [[University of Arizona]] and serves as the director of the Arizona Center for Mathematical Sciences.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Jerome V Moloney |url=https://profiles.arizona.edu/person/jvm2 |website=The university of Arizona}}</ref>

== Biography ==
Moloney earned his B.Sc. degree from [[University College Cork]], [[Ireland]], in 1970, and completed his Ph.D. at the [[University of Western Ontario]], [[Canada]], in 1976. From 1977 to 1979, he served as a [[research associate]] in physics at [[Bielefeld University|Universität Bielefeld]] in [[Bielefeld]], [[Germany]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=Jerome V. Moloney |url=https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/author/37272599600 |access-date=2025-03-06 |website=ieeexplore.ieee.org}}</ref><ref name=":2">{{Cite web | url=https://apps.dtic.mil/sti/tr/pdf/ADA601229.pdf | title=Report documentation page | website=apps.dtic.mil}}</ref>

In 1979, he joined the Optical Sciences Center, University of Arizona, as a research associate.<ref name=":1" /> From 1981 until 1984 he was a [[research assistant]] and associate professor in optical sciences at the University of Arizona.{{Dubious|date=March 2025|reason=This is different from the source used, it looks like date errors}} In 1984, he became a reader in physics at [[Heriot-Watt University]],<ref name=":1" /> till 1990. In 1990, he was appointed a full professor at the University of Arizona and became the director of the Arizona Center for Mathematical Sciences the same year.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":2" />{{Self-published inline|date=March 2025}}

== Main research topics ==
Moloney's research interests cover multiple topics in large-scale [[physics simulation]]s, [[applied mathematics]], [[photonics]], and nonlinear optics fields.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Predictive semiconductor laser design free of fit parameters |url=https://spie.org/news/0536-predictive-semiconductor-laser-design-free-of-fit-parameters |access-date=2025-03-06 |website=spie.org}}</ref> He, with colleagues at Arizona, suggested that the reason for the non-spreading propagation of X waves found by Di Trapani's was due to the interplay of Kerr nonlinearity and chromatic dispersion,<ref name=":3">{{Cite web | url=https://medical-imaging-research.org/papers_pdf/erasmo/physics_today_oct2004.pdf | title=Intense X−Shaped Pulses of Light Propagate Without Spreading in Water and Other Dispersive Media | website=medical-imaging-research.org}}</ref> and later, that optical carrier shock waves strongly influence long wavelength laser pulses propagating in the atmosphere.<ref name=":3" />

Moloney proposed the “[[Airy beam]]” to create a new method for guiding laser light. Combining an Airy beam with a high-intensity pulse beam, Moloney's team created curved plasma channels. By using the lens, these channels can be bent or straightened.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Merali |first=Zeeya |date=2009-04-09 |title=Bendy laser beams fired through the air |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/news.2009.360 |journal=Nature |language=en |doi=10.1038/news.2009.360 |issn=1476-4687|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The phenomenon propagated to ultra-intense self-bending Airy beams in transparent dielectric media.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Polynkin |first1=Pavel |last2=Kolesik |first2=Miroslav |last3=Moloney |first3=Jerome |last4=Siviloglou |first4=Georgios |last5=Christodoulides |first5=Demetrios |date=2010-09-01 |title=Extreme Nonlinear Optics with Ultra-Intense Self-Bending Airy Beams |url=https://opg.optica.org/opn/abstract.cfm?URI=opn-21-9-38 |journal=Optics and Photonics News |language=EN |volume=21 |issue=9 |pages=38–43 |doi=10.1364/OPN.21.9.000038 |issn=1541-3721|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Moloney in 1999–2000, with colleagues at the University of Arizona as described in [[Optics Letters]] and [[Physical Review Letters]], proposed and described a mechanism whereby multiple light filaments created by high-power lasers in the atmosphere could be sustained over long distances, a mechanism critical to the generation of laser lightning rods. The latter concept was further developed with colleagues from the [[University of Central Florida]], described in [[Nature Photonics]],<ref>{{Cite web |title=Lasers to control lightning strikes {{!}} Electro Optics |url=https://www.electrooptics.com/news/lasers-control-lightning-strikes |access-date=2025-03-06 |website=www.electrooptics.com}}</ref> and was recently implemented in a field experiment to divert lightning strikes away from buildings and populated areas.

Moloney, with the collaboration of a team of US and German researchers, established a rigorous theoretical foundation to describe how semiconductor lasers operate, transitioning this knowledge to the development of commercial semiconductor epitaxy design software for lasers and sensors. The team designed a series of continuous, room-temperature, vertical-external-cavity semiconductor laser sources ([[Vertical-external-cavity surface-emitting-laser|VECSEL]]) that deliver narrowband, milliwatt beams at terahertz-gap frequencies and a yellow laser wavelength for guidestar applications. Their devices incorporate a nonlinear optics element into the external-cavity laser. Moloney and his coworkers generated a narrowband emission at the uppermost frequencies of the terahertz gap and at the laser guidestar (yellow) wavelengths by mixing two IR beams. He proposed visible light VECSELs<ref>{{Cite web |title=Novel semiconductor lasers attractive for UV-visible applications |url=https://spie.org/news/1473-novel-semiconductor-lasers-attractive-for-uv-visible-applications |access-date=2025-03-06 |website=spie.org}}</ref>  as practical compact Guidestar laser sources and recognized the potential of room temperature, tunable terahertz external-cavity surface-emitting lasers (TECSELs) as a practical technology for astronomical observations.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Smart |first=Ashley G. |date=2011-02-01 |title=Room-temperature source delivers record-power terahertz beam |url=https://pubs.aip.org/physicstoday/article-abstract/64/2/13/413599/room-temperature-source-delivers-record-power?redirectedfrom=pdf |journal=Physics Today |volume=64 |issue=2 |pages=13–15 |doi=10.1063/1.3554308 |bibcode=2011PhT....64b..13S |issn=0031-9228|url-access=subscription }}</ref>
